company.name: Duckly
company.shortDescription: Duckly is an IDE plugin for developers that offers to talk, share their code, server, terminal, and collaborate in real-time services.
company.description: GitDuck is a video call tool built for developers that enables them to talk, share their code, and do pair programming with ease. An ideal tool for programmers since it is optimized for real-time code sharing, not for a grid of high-resolution videos like Zooms.

productsAndServices.description: An IDE plugin enabling developers to collaborate in real-time by sharing code, servers, terminals, and communicating via audio and video within their preferred IDE.
productsAndServices.name: Duckly IDE Plugin

productsAndServices.description: A web-based IDE embedded in Duckly's platform that allows users to join coding sessions and collaborate without installing any IDE plugins.
productsAndServices.name: Duckly Web IDE

productsAndServices.description: A terminal integration tool that allows developers to share terminal sessions securely during Duckly calls.
productsAndServices.name: Duckly Terminal Sharing

insights.title: Valuation increased across disclosed rounds
insights.statement: Known post-money valuation rose from $2,702,325 to $6,499,241, a 2.41x increase.
insights.implication: The disclosed financing history indicates a material valuation step-up between the earliest and latest rounds with known valuations.
caveats: Only rounds with a disclosed post-money valuation are compared.

insights.title: Sharp recent attention and growth momentum
insights.statement: Crunchbase scores growth at 65 (-1 over 90 days) and market heat at 68 (-11).
insights.implication: The company has recently become much more visible, but the scores should be treated as attention/activity indicators rather than revenue or clinical-performance metrics.
caveats: Crunchbase does not expose the complete weighting behind these proprietary scores.

insights.title: Competitive benchmark reflects the modeled peer set

insights.implication: These matches provide a starting point for comparing differentiation, scale, and shared specialties, but they should not be treated as a verified competitor set.
